content: Nigella sativa is an annual flowering plant that originates from Southwest Asia. It typically grows to a height of 20 to 30 centimeters and features finely divided, linear leaves that are not thread-like in appearance. The plant produces delicate flowers, which are usually pale blue and white in color, with five to ten petals. Its fruit is a large, inflated capsule made up of three to seven united follicles, each containing numerous seeds. These seeds are commonly used as a spice. The seeds of Nigella sativa are known by various names in different languages and cultures. In Hindi, they are called kalonji (कलौंजी or कलोंजी). In Hebrew, they are referred to as kezah (קצח). In Russian, they are known as charnushka, while in Turkish, they are called çörek otu. In Arabic, they are named habbah Albarakah (حبه البركة), meaning seeds of blessing, and in Persian, they are called siyah daneh (سیاه‌دانه). In English, the seeds are referred to as fennel flower, black caraway, nutmeg flower, Roman coriander, or black onion seed. However, some names, such as onion seed and black sesame, are misleading, as they refer to unrelated plants with similar-looking seeds. The term black cumin is also frequently used, but this can cause confusion, as it is also the name for a different spice, Bunium persicum. The seeds are sometimes simply called nigella or black seed. An old English name for the plant, gith, is now used for a different plant, the corn cockle. The variety of vernacular names for Nigella sativa reflects its relatively recent introduction as a widely used spice in English-speaking regions, primarily through immigrants from areas where the plant is well-known. As its use becomes more widespread, it is likely that one unambiguous name will become dominant. The seeds of Nigella sativa have a pungent, bitter taste and a faint aroma reminiscent of strawberries. They are primarily used in candies and liquors. A type of naan bread known as Peshawari naan is often topped with kalonji seeds. In herbal medicine, Nigella sativa is recognized for its antihypertensive, carminative, and anthelmintic properties. The seeds are even consumed by elephants to aid digestion. Historical Context Archaeological evidence regarding the earliest cultivation of Nigella sativa is limited. However, seeds of this plant have been discovered at several ancient Egyptian sites, including the tomb of Tutankhamun. While its exact role in Egyptian culture remains unclear, the inclusion of items in a pharaoh's tomb was typically intended to assist in the afterlife. The earliest written reference to Nigella sativa appears in the Old Testament, in the Book of Isaiah, where its harvesting is contrasted with that of wheat (Isaiah 28:25, 27). Easton's Bible Dictionary confirms that the Hebrew word ketzah undoubtedly refers to Nigella sativa. During classical times, Nigella sativa was a traditional condiment in the Old World, and its black seeds were extensively used to flavor food. In the Unani Tibb system of medicine, Nigella sativa has been regarded as a valuable remedy for various diseases. Ibn Sina (Avicenna), renowned for his medical encyclopedia The Canon of Medicine, described Nigella sativa as a seed that stimulates the body's energy and aids recovery from fatigue and despondency. He attributed several therapeutic effects to the seeds, including benefits for digestive disorders, gynecological diseases, and respiratory conditions. Nigella sativa is also listed among the natural remedies in Tibb e Nabwi (Prophetic Medicine), with a tradition stating, Hold on to the use of the black seeds, for in it is healing for all diseases except death (Sahih Bukhari, vol. 7, book 71, 592). The seeds have been traditionally used in the Middle East and Southeast Asia to treat ailments such as asthma, bronchitis, rheumatism, and other inflammatory diseases. They are also used to enhance milk production in nursing mothers, promote digestion, and combat parasitic infections. The oil extracted from the seeds has been applied to treat skin conditions like eczema and boils, as well as to alleviate cold symptoms. Use in Folk Medicine Nigella sativa has been used for centuries in Asia, the Middle East, and Africa for medicinal purposes, both as a herb and in the form of pressed oil. It has been traditionally employed to address a wide range of conditions, including respiratory health, gastrointestinal health, kidney and liver function, circulatory and immune system support, and overall well-being. In Islamic tradition, it is considered one of the most potent forms of healing medicine. Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said that the black seed can cure every disease except death, as mentioned in a hadith. This Biblical herb, often used in breads and cakes, has been employed medicinally to purge the body of worms and parasites. An Arab proverb refers to it as the medicine for every disease except death. The seeds have a hot taste and are sometimes mixed with peppercorns in Europe. Black cumin oil contains nigellone, which has been shown to protect guinea pigs from histamine-induced bronchial spasms, potentially explaining its use in relieving symptoms of asthma, bronchitis, and coughs. The presence of beta-sitosterol, an anti-tumor sterol, supports its traditional use in treating abscesses and tumors of the abdomen, eyes, and liver.
